title: Rōma est magna
can: Read and write simple sentences about Rome, and pronounce Latin the way Romans did.
doneText: You can now read simple Latin sentences, spot plurals and pronounce Latin like a Roman.

discover.intro: Your first Latin. There's no word for "the" anywhere. See what changes when there's more than one.
discover.question: What changes when there is more than one?
options: The -a ending becomes -ae, on the noun and on the describing word, and est becomes sunt.
A word for "many" is added at the start.
Nothing changes: Latin shows plurals from context only.
discover.nudge: Not quite. Compare puella with puellae, and laeta with laetae.
discover.reveal: Latin has no "the" or "a": puella is "the girl" or "a girl". For more than one, the ending changes, the describing word changes to match, and est (is) becomes sunt (are). Two hooks:

blocks.text: Spanish es and son come straight from Latin est and sunt. Spot the family: Latin sum, es, est; Spanish soy, eres, es; Italian sono, sei, è.
No articles: Rōma est magna is "Rome is great", and puella est laeta can be "the girl" or "a girl is happy". Choose whichever English sounds natural.

blocks.title: The describing word follows its noun
blocks.note: Parva, magna, longa and laeta take the same ending as their noun. That's how Latin shows which word describes which, even when they're far apart.

blocks.text: Most -a nouns are feminine. A few are masculine because of what they mean: agricola (farmer), nauta (sailor), poēta (poet). Romans assumed those were men's jobs.

exercises.why: -a for one, -ae for more than one: viae.
Īnsula = island, parva = small. Add "the" or "a" as English needs.
Sunt and laetae are plural, so puellae.

Tap the word that is wrong.
exercises.why: Viae is plural, so its describing word is plural too: longae.

exercises.prompt: Match each Latin word with its Spanish descendant.

exercises.why: Rōma magna est, with the verb last, sounds very Roman. Both orders are right.

exercises.prompt: How did Cicero say his own name?
exercises.why: In classical Latin c is always hard, like k. The soft sounds came later, in Church Latin and in Italian.
Sum, es, est, sumus: we are.
Frīgida = cold. English frigid and Spanish frío come from the same root.

exercises.prompt: Tap the word that is wrong.
Spanish soy, eres, es comes from which Latin verb?
exercises.why: Spanish ser grew out of Latin esse (sum, es, est) and sedēre (to sit).

write.title: Write it in Latin
write.task: Describe a Roman street in three short sentences: the road, the statues and the girls. Use est and sunt.
write.model: Via est longa. Statuae sunt antīquae et pulchrae. Puellae sunt laetae.
checklist: One thing: est. More than one: sunt
No word for "the" needed. Et means and

boss.title: Reading: a Roman street
boss.persona: You are Magistra Līvia, a warm Latin teacher. The learner has just read their first Latin: est, sunt, sum, nouns ending in -a and -ae, and describing words (magna, parva, longa, laeta, pulchra, antīqua, nova, clāra). Chat in English and give very short Latin sentences using only these for them to translate or answer.

choices: Rome is great.
Rome is small.
Magna is big or great. Small is parva.
The Romans are great.
Rōma is the city, and est means one thing: is.
The roads are long and old.
The road is long and old.
Viae and sunt are plural: the roads are.
The roads are new and long.
Antīquae is old. New would be novae.

turns.npc: Puella est laeta, sed via nōn est longa.
choices: The girl is happy, but the road is not long.
The girl is happy and the road is long.
Sed is but, and nōn is not.
The girls are happy, but the road is not long.
Puella and est are singular: one girl.
The island of Sicily is famous.
Sicily is a small island.
Clāra is famous. Small would be parva.
The islands of Sicily are famous.
Īnsula and est are singular: one island.

boss.closingEn: Excellent! You've read your first Latin story.
boss.chatOpeningEn: Hello! What is Rome like? Try answering in Latin: Rōma est…
